title: It Came Upon the Midnight Clear
about: Edmund Sears wrote the poem in 1849. It was first printed in The Christian Register, in Boston, on December 29, 1849. Richard Storrs Willis published the tune a year later, as a study for choirs called Carol. Hymnals in the United States set the poem to it, and it became a well loved carol.
funFact: In Britain, the same words are usually sung to a different tune, Noel, which Arthur Sullivan arranged from an English melody.

practice.text: Play the first three bars with the right hand alone, and let the song wait for each note.
Play bars 9 to 13 with the right hand alone, where the tune drops and climbs back.
Now the left hand alone. It holds one fifth or one note at a time, and stays in one place.
Put both hands together on the first five bars.
Play the whole song with both hands at full speed.

tips.text: Lift the thumb off G a moment early. The little finger then has time to reach the high E.
The tune drops a whole octave here. Lift the hand off the high E, and land the thumb on the low one.
Count six beats in a bar: long, short, long, short. The tune sways like a lullaby.

tricky.text: After the short rest, finger 5 lands on the high E. Fingers 4, 3 and 2 then walk down to A.
Finger 2 plays A twice, and finger 3 steps up to B. Then fingers 2 and 1 walk down to G.
The same shape as bar 6: finger 5 on the high E, then 4, 3 and 2 down to A.

practice.text: Play the left hand alone. A bass note comes first, then the rest of its chord.
Play the right hand alone on the first five bars, slowly.
Play bars 9 to 13 with the right hand alone, where the tune drops and climbs.
Join the hands on bars 1 to 5.
Play the whole song with both hands at full speed.

tips.text: On the second C, swap finger 4 for the thumb. Fingers 2 and 3 then reach D and E.
Use the long chord in bar 5 to get the hand ready for the high E.
The tune climbs through F sharp and G sharp. Let it grow a little louder up to the high E.

tricky.text: Fingers 3, 4 and 5 climb to A, B and C. Then finger 5 moves on up to the high E.
The tune drops from the high E to the low one. Then the thumb slides up to F sharp, and finger 2 takes G sharp.
Fingers 4, 3, 2 and 1 walk down from D to A. Then finger 3 takes B, so finger 2 lands on A.

practice.text: Play the Alberti bass alone until it rolls by itself: low, high, middle, high.
Play the right hand alone on bars 9 to 13, and pass the thumb under on the way up.
Play the right hand's thirds and sixths alone, and press both notes of each pair as one.
Play the whole song with both hands at three quarters speed.
Now play it at full speed, with the pedal.

tips.text: Keep the Alberti bass soft, so the tune floats above it.
Climb E, F sharp and G sharp with fingers 1, 2 and 3, then pass the thumb under to A.
The tune is the top note of each pair, so let the upper finger lead.

tricky.text: The pairs change shape: 1 and 3 for a third, 1 and 5 for a sixth. The thumb walks down to B, then up to D.
Thirds on F and A, then fingers 2 and 4 step up to G and B and back. The thumb reaches down to B at the end.
The thumb moves from G up to A. Fingers 2 to 5 then climb to E, with finger 3 on both Cs.

practice.text: Play the stride bass alone: jump down for the octave, then back up for the chord.
Play the right hand's chords alone, and let the top finger sing the tune.
Join the hands on the third phrase, bars 9 to 13, where the tune drops and climbs.
Play the whole song with both hands at three quarters speed.
Now play it at full speed, and make the last chord ring.

tips.text: In stride, look at the bass note and let the hand find the chord by feel.
Play the top note of each chord a little louder than the others.
A short rest comes before each upbeat. Use it to move the hand to the next chord.

tricky.text: Another four-note chord, G, B, D and G, with the little finger on top. Lift it in the rest before the upbeat.
Spread the hand over four notes: D, G, B and D. Then lift it and land the thumb on the G.
Finger 3 sings A over E and G. Then the thumb drops to B under F and G, and finger 3 keeps the tune's G.
